findings.claim: US export controls aim to restrict PRC access to advanced chips, AI computing power, and EDA tools.
US export controls include restrictions on access through third-party countries and cloud computing services.
Chinese entities may seek overseas cloud services if the performance gap between locally available and foreign AI chips grows.
Current US export controls do not explicitly regulate the provision of cloud computing services to prevent access to controlled chips.
Restricting foreign access to US technology may incentivize other nations to build technology infrastructure using non-American components.
US graduate programs have a high percentage of foreign nationals.
Research papers co-authored by researchers from the U.S. and China receive more citations than those that do not.
The AI diffusion framework categorizes the U.S. and 18 partners as Tier 1 nations with unrestricted access.
The AI diffusion framework categorizes most nations as Tier 2 with controlled access via licensing.
The AI diffusion framework categorizes strategic competitors as Tier 3 nations facing restrictions.
Semiconductors are increasingly subject to non-tariff measures including export restrictions.
Export restrictions on AI-enabling goods may jeopardize the global dissemination of AI.
Geopolitical restrictions act as a barrier to international data-sharing and collaboration in healthcare AI.
Data silos resulting from restricted collaboration may limit innovation and generalizability in healthcare AI.
There is an ongoing debate regarding the balance between technological sovereignty and the necessity of international collaboration for innovation and skills development.

The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security implemented controls on the export, re-export, and in-country transfer of weights for closed-weight AI models trained with 10^26 computational operations or more.
The Foreign Direct Product Rule extends controls to model weights produced abroad using advanced computing chips manufactured with U.S. technology or equipment.

U.S. Infrastructure as a Service providers are subject to Know Your Customer guidance to identify if they are providing compute clusters to train advanced AI models for foreign entities or their U.S. subsidiaries.
Chinese companies like Alibaba and Baidu have begun training AI models using internally designed chips.
Baidu uses the Kunlun P800 chip for training AI models.
U.S. export controls were estimated to provide the U.S. with a four-year hardware lead in training frontier models as of October 2023.
There is reportedly little to no U.S. hardware lead over China in model inference.
China produces twice as many research papers as the United States on the topics of chip design and production.
Chinese researchers continue to participate in international AI research conferences.
Chinese researchers maintain access to open-source models developed by Western firms.
The Chinese government has committed massive resources to indigenous semiconductor research.
The Chinese government has increased subsidized development efforts for semiconductors.
Chinese AI developers face challenges in transitioning Large Language Model development to domestic hardware ecosystems.
TSMC will suspend the production of AI semiconductors at the 7-nanometer node or smaller for Chinese clients.
Research organizations outside the U.S. face challenges regarding the extraterritorial application of U.S. export controls.
The U.S. deemed re-export rule complicates collaborations between non-U.S. research organizations and researchers affiliated with other companies or universities.
Students and researchers at non-U.S. institutions may require access to U.S.-origin technology or software to conduct research.
Compliance with U.S. regulations regarding U.S.-origin technology is a challenge for non-U.S. research organizations.
U.S. export regulations define an export to include the disclosure of technology, software source code, or technical data to a foreign national anywhere in the world.
The Fundamental Research Exclusion does not apply to export-controlled items, technology, or technical data received from third parties.
The release of controlled technical data to non-U.S. nationals can be deemed an export to their home jurisdiction.
Releasing controlled technical data to non-U.S. nationals may require authorization from the Bureau of Industry and Security.

unclosed_gaps: Empirical data or case studies specifically documenting changes in academic publication output from universities outside the US (e.g., in China or Tier 2/3 nations) directly attributable to export controls.
Specific evidence on how academic researchers outside the US have altered their research agendas or collaboration patterns due to compute access limitations.
Quantitative metrics or surveys regarding the actual impact of export controls on the ability of non-US academic institutions to secure high-performance computing resources for AI research.
